problem_statement: The paper frames dynamic portfolio optimization as finding an investment trajectory over multiple rebalancing dates that maximizes return while minimizing risk, with transaction costs included. It treats the task as a rebalancing problem over time rather than a one-shot portfolio choice.
problem_statement_quotes: In this paper; we explore DPO a variant of the stan- dard portfolio optimization problem, where the portfolio (with Na assets) is rebalanced at certain dates (over Nt dates) . Rebalancing the portfolio introduces transaction costs, C(2) , that we also consider in the problem:

Building upon the foundational work of Harry Markowitz in Modern Portfolio Theory [31], portfolio optimization has become a widely studied mathematical problem in finance It consists in finding the investment trajectory m2 that maximizes the return of the port fo- lio, F() _ while minimizing the risk associated with it, R()
classical_baseline: The paper compares against classical optimization solvers for the QUBO formulation, especially Gurobi, DOCPLEX, exhaustive search, and GEKKO. It also uses Gurobi as the main classical reference because it performs best in their benchmarks.
classical_baseline_quotes: We first benchmark four classical reference solvers: eX- haustive search; Gurobi [36], IBM Decision Optimization CPLEX (DOCPLEX) [37]. and GEKKO [38] (details on Appendix E)_
classical_difficulty: The paper says traditional classical algorithms often struggle with large-scale DPO data, and that the objective becomes harder because transaction costs couple different time steps so the problem can no longer be solved independently at each time step. It also notes that the Sharpe-ratio-based objective is challenging because of its inverse power dependence on n.
classical_difficulty_quotes: Optimizing a DPO objective function directly based on the Sharpe ratio can be challenging due to the inverse power dependence On n in Eq: (1)_
extraction_notes: Motivation is explicit in the introduction; paper is partly methodological but does state the finance problem and classical difficulty clearly.
